sessions.title: What Is a Computer?
indicators: Explain that a computer is an electronic device that works with information
Identify that computers can be used at home, school, offices, and shops
Distinguish between a computer and other electronic devices (TV, radio, phone)
Work in groups to list places where computers are used (collaboration)
Use digital pictures to identify different types of computers (digital literacy)
Discuss the importance of computers in everyday life (critical thinking, citizenship)
sessions.content:
Hello, Computer!

A computer is a clever machine that helps us with information. It can take in data (like numbers, words, or pictures), process it, and give us back something useful – just like a smart helper.

1. What Computers Do

Computers can:

  • Write letters and stories
  • Draw pictures and play music
  • Solve maths problems
  • Connect to the internet to find information and talk to people far away

A computer is different from a television or a radio because a TV only shows pictures and a radio only plays sounds – a computer can do many things and let you control what happens.

Activity 1 – Computer or Not?
Look at a set of pictures (or real objects): desktop computer, laptop, tablet, smartphone, calculator, TV, radio, microwave. With a partner, decide which are computers and which are not. Explain your choices. (collaboration, critical thinking)

2. Where Do We Find Computers?

Computers are everywhere! They are in:

  • Schools – in the computer lab, the headmaster’s office, and sometimes in your classroom
  • Homes – a family desktop, a parent’s laptop or tablet
  • Hospitals – to keep patient records
  • Shops and banks – to calculate bills, print receipts, and keep money safe
  • Airports and stations – to check tickets and schedules

Activity 2 – Computer Hunt
Walk around the school (or think about your community) and make a list of all the places you have seen a computer being used. Share your list with the class and count who found the most. (collaboration, communication)

Digital corner: If a tablet or computer is available, look at photos of different computer types: desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone, smartwatch. Discuss how they are the same and different. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.1

  1. What is a computer?
  2. Name two things a computer can do that a radio cannot.
  3. Write down three places where computers are used.
  4. Draw a picture of a computer you have seen before. Label the screen and keyboard.

sessions.title: Parts of a Computer – Hardware
indicators: Identify the main parts of a desktop computer: system unit, monitor, keyboard, mouse
Name additional parts: printer, speakers, webcam, headphone
Explain that these parts are called ‘hardware’ because you can touch them
Work in pairs to match hardware names to pictures (collaboration)
Use a digital simulation to explore computer parts (digital literacy)
Handle hardware gently and discuss the importance of taking care of devices (personal development)
sessions.content:
The Body of a Computer – Hardware

Everything you can touch on a computer is called hardware. These are the physical parts you can see and feel.

1. Main Parts of a Desktop Computer

  • System Unit (the brain): The big box that contains the computer’s brain and heart. It processes all the information.
  • Monitor (the face): Looks like a TV screen. It shows you pictures, words, and videos.
  • Keyboard (the hands): Has many buttons called keys. You press them to type letters, numbers, and give commands.
  • Mouse (the pointing finger): A small device you move with your hand. It moves a pointer (cursor) on the screen so you can click on things.

Activity 1 – Build a Computer
Use paper cut‑outs or a puzzle of a computer. In pairs, put the parts together and label them. Say aloud what each part does. (collaboration, communication)

2. Other Hardware Parts

  • Printer: Puts words and pictures from the computer onto paper.
  • Speakers: Play sounds and music.
  • Headphones: Let you listen privately.
  • Webcam: A small camera that takes pictures or videos of you.

Activity 2 – Hardware Touch and Tell
If real hardware is available, the teacher will pass around the parts. Touch them gently and name them. Always hold hardware with both hands and don’t drop it. (personal development)

Digital corner: Use a computer parts labelling game online (or an app) to drag names to the correct parts. (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.2

  1. What is hardware?
  2. Match the part to its job: (a) Monitor (b) Keyboard (c) Mouse (d) Printer → (i) prints on paper (ii) shows pictures (iii) moves the pointer (iv) types letters.
  3. Draw a simple desktop computer and label four parts.
  4. Why should we handle computer parts gently?

sessions.title: Software – What Makes the Computer Work
indicators: Explain that software is a set of instructions that tells hardware what to do
Give examples of software: operating system, games, word processor
Understand that without software, hardware cannot work
Collaborate to sort pictures into ‘Hardware’ and ‘Software’ (collaboration)
Use a simple drawing or educational app to experience software (digital literacy)
Appreciate that both hardware and software are needed together (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
The Invisible Helper – Software

Hardware alone is like a body without a brain. Software is the instructions (programs) that tell the computer what to do. You cannot touch software, but you can see it working on the screen.

1. Types of Software

  • Operating System: The boss software that runs the whole computer. It makes the mouse, keyboard and screen work together. Examples: Windows, Android.
  • Application Software (Apps): Programs that help you do specific tasks – write a story (word processor), draw a picture (Paint), play a game, or learn with an educational app.

Activity 1 – Software in Action
The teacher will open a simple program (like a painting app or a word processor). Watch how clicking the mouse makes things happen. Those are software instructions! (critical thinking)

2. Hardware + Software = Working Computer

Think of a pencil (hardware) and your brain (software). Without your brain telling the pencil what to write, the pencil does nothing. A computer needs both.

Activity 2 – Sort the Cards
You will get cards with pictures or words: monitor, keyboard, Paint program, game, printer, Windows. In groups, sort them into ‘Hardware’ and ‘Software’ and explain your choice. (collaboration, communication)

Digital corner: On a tablet, open a drawing app. Use your finger to draw a simple picture. Discuss: what hardware and software are you using? (digital literacy)

Exercise 1.3

  1. What is software?
  2. Is a computer game hardware or software? Why?
  3. Write the name of one software you have seen or used.
  4. Explain why a computer cannot work with hardware alone.

sessions.title: Starting and Shutting Down a Computer Properly
indicators: Identify the power button on a system unit and monitor
Follow the correct steps to start (boot) a computer
Follow the correct steps to shut down a computer
Work in pairs to practise the steps (collaboration)
Use a computer simulation to practise booting up (digital literacy)
Discuss the importance of shutting down correctly to protect the computer (personal development)
sessions.content:
Power On, Power Off – The Right Way

Just like you wake up and go to bed, a computer must be started and stopped in a careful way so it stays healthy.

1. Starting the Computer (Booting)

  1. Check that the computer is plugged into the power socket and the switch is on.
  2. Press the power button on the monitor first (a small light comes on).
  3. Press the power button on the system unit (you will hear a fan and see lights).
  4. Wait patiently – the computer loads its software. You will see the desktop screen when it’s ready.

Activity 1 – Boot‑up Role Play
In pairs, one person acts as the monitor, the other as the system unit. Say the steps aloud and pretend to press the buttons. Swap roles. (collaboration, communication)

2. Shutting Down (Turning Off)

Do NOT just press the power button! That can damage the computer.

  1. Click the Start button (usually at the bottom‑left corner of the screen).
  2. Click the Power icon.
  3. Click Shut down.
  4. Wait until the screen goes dark and the computer becomes silent.
  5. Then switch off the monitor and unplug if needed.

Activity 2 – Shutdown Practice
Using a real computer if available (or a paper printout of the screen), point to where you must click. The teacher will guide you through the real shutdown process. (critical thinking)

Digital corner: Use an online simulation (if available) that lets you practise starting and shutting down a virtual computer. (digital literacy)

Discussion: What might happen if you pull the plug while the computer is working? (You could lose your work or break the computer.)

Exercise 2.1

  1. Which button do you press first to start a computer?
  2. Write the steps to shut down a computer correctly.
  3. Why is it important to wait for the computer to finish shutting down?
  4. Draw a simple power button symbol.

sessions.title: Using the Mouse – Click, Double‑click, Drag
indicators: Hold and move the mouse correctly to control the pointer
Perform single‑click to select items
Perform double‑click to open items
Perform drag and drop to move items
Work in pairs to practise mouse skills using a simple game (collaboration)
Use a digital mouse‑skill training program (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Point, Click, Drag – Mastering the Mouse

The mouse is your finger inside the computer. Learning to use it well is the first big step in becoming a computer champion.

1. Holding and Moving the Mouse

Place your hand gently on the mouse. Your index finger rests on the left button, middle finger on the right button. Slide the mouse on a flat surface – the pointer (arrow) on the screen moves just like your hand.

Activity 1 – Mouse Maze
If a computer is available, open a simple drawing program or a mouse‑skill game. Practise moving the pointer into a target without clicking. (personal development)

2. Click, Double‑click, Right‑click

  • Single‑click (click): Press and release the left button once. It selects an item (highlights it).
  • Double‑click: Quickly press the left button twice. It opens a file, folder or program.
  • Right‑click: Press the right button once. It shows a menu with extra choices.

Activity 2 – Click Practice
On a desktop, the teacher will create a folder with many icons. Practise single‑clicking to select, double‑clicking to open a picture, and right‑clicking to see the menu. (collaboration – help each other)

3. Drag and Drop

Point to an item, press and hold the left button, move the mouse to a new spot, then release the button. The item moves there. It’s like picking up a pencil and placing it somewhere else.

Activity 3 – Jigsaw Puzzle
Play an online jigsaw puzzle where you drag pieces into place. (digital literacy)

Exercise 2.2

  1. What part of your hand should you use to press the left mouse button?
  2. What is the difference between a single‑click and a double‑click?
  3. Write the step you do to move an icon from one side of the screen to the other.
  4. Draw a simple mouse and label the left and right buttons.

sessions.title: Using the Keyboard – Letters, Numbers and Special Keys
indicators: Identify the letter keys, number keys, spacebar, Enter key, and Backspace key
Type simple words and short sentences using the keyboard
Use the Shift key to make capital letters
Work in pairs to practise typing using a typing game (collaboration)
Use a digital keyboarding app to build speed (digital literacy)
Develop proper sitting posture and finger placement for healthy typing (personal development)
sessions.content:
Your Fingers Do the Talking – The Keyboard

The keyboard lets you put words and numbers into the computer. It has many keys arranged in a special order called QWERTY (named after the first six letter keys).

1. Important Keys

  • Letter keys: A to Z – for typing words.
  • Number keys: 0 to 9 – above the letters.
  • Spacebar: The long key at the bottom. Puts a space between words.
  • Enter key: Moves the cursor to the next line (like pressing ‘new paragraph’).
  • Backspace key: Erases the letter to the left of the cursor.
  • Shift key: Hold it down and press a letter to make a capital letter.

Activity 1 – Find the Key
In pairs, one person calls out a key name (e.g., “Spacebar!”, “Letter G!”, “Enter!”) and the other points to it on a real keyboard or a large paper keyboard printout. Swap roles. (collaboration)

2. Typing Your First Words

Sit up straight. Keep your feet flat on the floor. Place your fingers on the middle row of letters (the home row).

Try typing: cat dog sun

Remember to press the spacebar with your thumb between words.

Activity 2 – Name Typing
Open a word processing program (e.g., Microsoft Word, Google Docs, or a simple text editor). Type your name. Press Enter. Type your friend’s name. Use the Shift key to make the first letter capital. (personal development – patience and good posture)

Digital corner: Use a child‑friendly typing game (like Dance Mat Typing) to practise finding letters quickly. (digital literacy)

Exercise 2.3

  1. What does the Spacebar do?
  2. Which key do you press to erase a mistake?
  3. Type this on a keyboard (if available): “My name is ____.”
  4. What finger should you use to press the spacebar?

sessions.title: What Is the Internet?
indicators: Explain that the internet connects computers all over the world
Give examples of what we can do on the internet (learn, play, talk to people)
Identify a web browser icon (e.g., Chrome, Edge) and a website address
Work in groups to list good reasons to use the internet (collaboration)
Use a teacher‑guided internet search for a simple topic (digital literacy)
Discuss that not everything on the internet is true or safe (critical thinking, citizenship)
sessions.content:
The World Wide Web – The Internet

The internet is like a giant spider web that connects millions of computers all over the world. Through the internet, you can visit places, read stories, watch videos, and even talk to someone far away.

1. What Can You Do on the Internet?

  • Find information: Look up facts about animals, countries, or your favourite sport.
  • Watch and learn: See educational videos on YouTube Kids (with permission).
  • Communicate: Send a message or an e‑mail to a friend or teacher.
  • Play educational games: Practise maths, spelling, and puzzles online.

Activity 1 – Internet Uses Brainstorm
In small groups, draw a mind map. In the middle write “Internet”. Around it, draw or write as many things as you can that people do on the internet. Share your mind map with the class. (collaboration, creativity)

2. How to Get to the Internet

We use a program called a web browser to open the internet. Common browsers: Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge. The browser has an address bar where you type a website address (URL), for example: www.kiddle.co (a safe search engine for kids).

Activity 2 – Guided Search
With the teacher leading, open a browser and type a safe website. Look at the pictures and words. (digital literacy)

Critical thinking: If you read something on the internet that says “Lions can fly”, do you believe it? Always check with a trusted adult or book.

Exercise 3.1

  1. What is the internet?
  2. Name two things you can do on the internet.
  3. Draw the icon of your school’s web browser.
  4. Why should you not believe everything you read on the internet?

sessions.title: Staying Safe Online
indicators: Explain the importance of never sharing personal information online (name, address, school, phone number)
Recognise that strangers online are still strangers – never meet them
Identify safe websites and apps that are made for children
Role‑play what to do if something scary or strange appears online (creativity, collaboration)
Use a digital ‘safety checklist’ to discuss online behaviour (digital literacy)
Develop a personal ‘Internet Safety Pledge’ (personal development)
sessions.content:
Be Smart, Be Safe – Online Safety Rules

The internet is amazing, but just like the real world, there are things we must be careful about. Follow these rules every time you are online.

1. The Golden Rules of Online Safety

  1. Keep personal information private: Never tell anyone online your full name, home address, school name, phone number, or password. It’s like giving a stranger a key to your house.
  2. Strangers are strangers – even online: If someone you don’t know sends you a message, do not reply. Tell a trusted adult immediately.
  3. Stick to safe sites: Only visit websites and apps your teacher or parents have approved.
  4. If something feels wrong, stop and tell: If you see a picture or message that makes you feel scared, uncomfortable or confused, close the screen (or turn off the monitor) and tell an adult right away.

Activity 1 – Safety Skit
In groups, act out a short scene where one child gets a message from a stranger online. What should they do? Show the correct steps. (creativity, collaboration)

2. My Internet Safety Pledge

Write down your own promise:

“I will not share my personal information online. I will only use sites my teacher says are okay. I will tell an adult if I see something that worries me.”

Decorate your pledge and sign it. (personal development)

Digital corner: Look at a children’s safety website together (e.g., the Child Online Protection page). Discuss the pictures. (digital literacy)

Exercise 3.2

  1. Why shouldn’t you tell your school’s name to someone online?
  2. What should you do if a stranger talks to you on the internet?
  3. Write down two things that are safe to share online and two things that are not.
  4. Draw a poster with one important online safety rule.

sessions.title: Healthy Computer Habits
indicators: Identify correct sitting posture when using a computer
Explain the 20‑20‑20 rule to rest the eyes (every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds)
List good habits: take breaks, don’t eat or drink near the computer, keep the computer room clean
Demonstrate correct posture in pairs and correct each other (collaboration)
Use a simple timer app to practise taking breaks (digital literacy)
Reflect on how healthy habits make learning more enjoyable (personal development)
sessions.content:
Feel Good While You Compute

Using a computer is fun, but if we sit the wrong way or use it for too long, our bodies can get tired or sore. Healthy habits keep us safe and comfortable.

1. Sitting Right – Posture

  • Your back should be straight and supported by the chair.
  • Your feet flat on the floor (not dangling).
  • The top of the screen should be at your eye level – you shouldn’t look up or down too much.
  • Your wrists should be straight while typing, not bent.

Activity 1 – Posture Check
In pairs, sit at a desk (or pretend one). Check your partner’s back, feet, and eye level. Gently remind them if they are slouching. (collaboration, communication)

2. Resting Your Eyes – The 20‑20‑20 Rule

Staring at a screen too long can make your eyes tired. Remember: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away (about 6 metres) for 20 seconds. Blink a lot!

Activity 2 – Timer Break
The teacher sets a 20‑minute timer. When it rings, stand up, stretch, look out the window and count to 20. (personal development)

3. Computer Room Manners

  • No eating or drinking near the computer – crumbs and liquids can damage it.
  • Wash your hands before using the keyboard to keep it clean.
  • Keep your computer area tidy – no books or papers on the keyboard.

Digital corner: Use a simple timer app on a tablet to remind you to take a break. (digital literacy)

Exercise 4.1

  1. Why is it important to sit up straight when using a computer?
  2. What does the 20‑20‑20 rule mean?
  3. Give two reasons why you should not eat at the computer.
  4. Draw a person sitting correctly at a computer. Add labels for back and feet.

sessions.title: Being a Responsible Computer User
indicators: Explain what it means to be responsible: taking care of devices, respecting others’ work
Never delete or change someone else’s file without permission
Understand that copying someone’s digital work as your own is wrong (digital respect)
Discuss class rules for using shared computers (collaboration, citizenship)
Use a shared device in turn and log off properly (personal development)
Appreciate that computers are tools for learning and should be used kindly (personal development)
sessions.content:
Good Digital Citizens

Being a good computer user means treating the computer and other people’s work with respect – just like you would treat a library book or a friend’s toy.

1. Respect the Hardware

  • Handle the mouse and keyboard gently – no banging.
  • Don’t pull on cables or press the screen with your finger (it can damage the monitor).
  • If something breaks or doesn’t work, tell the teacher instead of trying to fix it yourself.

Activity 1 – Class Computer Rules Poster
As a class, make a list of five rules for the computer lab or tablet time. Write or draw them on a big poster and hang it on the wall. Everyone signs the bottom. (collaboration, citizenship)

2. Respect Others’ Digital Work

If someone has saved a drawing or a story, never delete it or write over it without asking. Imagine if someone erased your best picture! If you find a file that isn’t yours, leave it alone.

Activity 2 – Share and Take Turns
When using a shared computer, practise waiting for your turn. When you finish, close your program but don’t shut down the computer – log off your account if needed so the next person can start fresh. (personal development)

Digital corner: If each pupil has a personal folder, practise saving a short sentence in your own folder and not opening others’ folders. (digital literacy)

Exercise 4.2

  1. What should you do if you accidentally spill water near the computer?
  2. Why shouldn’t you open a file that belongs to your friend without asking?
  3. Write one rule you think is the most important for the computer lab.
  4. How can you be a good digital citizen at school?
